Open-Weight LLM Fine-Tuning Defenses
are Susceptible to Simple Attacks

Kevin Kuo    Virginia Smith ††thanks: These authors contributed equally.    Chhavi Yadav11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University  Simons Institute, UC Berkeley
Abstract

Recent defenses for safeguarding open-weight large language models (LLMs) are intended to prevent adversarial usage (Tamirisa et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). Underlying these defenses is an assumption that new harmful behavior is learned through fine-tuning rather than elicited by jailbreaking the model. Yet, pretrained LLMs already encode substantial harmful knowledge across many domains, which raises an important question: can an adversary jailbreak safeguarded models, to achieve harmful usage without fine-tuning at all? In this paper, we show that open-weight safeguards are susceptible to simpler strategies that, despite being well known, have not been systematically evaluated against these safeguards. Specifically, we evaluate two low-cost attacks–abliteration and prefilling–that do not rely on gradient-based optimization. Across three harmfulness evaluation benchmarks (BeaverTails, HarmBench, and AdvBench), these attacks increase attack success rates against safeguarded open-weight models from below 10% to a range of 16%-96%. To mitigate this vulnerability, we introduce abliteration-resistant tuning (ART), which incorporates an abliteration-based objective into training. ART can be layered onto existing defenses and reduces the success rates of abliteration, prefilling, and their combination by 10%-20%. These findings indicate that the attack surface for open-weight models is broader than previously characterized, and that evaluations of safeguarding defenses should incorporate a more diverse set of attack strategies beyond adversarial fine-tuning.

1 Introduction

Open-weight large language models (LLMs) bring substantial benefits to society such as enabling downstream customization, self-hosting for privacy, and open research (Minaee et al., 2024). However, they also significantly increase the potential for adversarial misuse. As a natural worst-case threat, an adversary can fine-tune the model for any harmful task/domain of its choice (Wallace et al., 2025). Safeguards against these fine-tuning attacks are an emerging line of work: tamper-resistant (Tamirisa et al., 2025) and self-destructing (Wang et al., 2025) models are two prominent examples.

Underlying this threat model is an implicit assumption that harmful behavior will be learned through downstream fine-tuning. However, pretrained LLMs contain broad knowledge relevant to many harmful tasks – even in domain-specific evaluations, baseline models achieve non-trivial harmfulness without any fine-tuning (Tamirisa et al., 2025). Thus, fine-tuning by adversaries often serves to remove refusal mechanisms rather than introduce new harmful capabilities (Lermen et al., 2023; Qi et al., 2024; Yi et al., 2024), raising a broader question about the robustness of safeguarded models:

Can an adversary bypass fine-tuning safeguards by simply eliciting already-present knowledge?

In this paper, we show that indeed, two inference-time attacks – Abliteration and Prefilling – can jailbreak safeguarded models without fine-tuning at all. Against two representative fine-tuning safeguards (TAR (Tamirisa et al., 2025) and SEAM (Wang et al., 2025)), these attacks achieve ASRs (attack success rates) ranging from 16% to 96% across benchmarks (BeaverTails, HarmBench, and AdvBench) and model architectures (Llama, Qwen, Gemma). While Abliteration and Prefilling are individually known attacks, their effectiveness against these safeguards has not been characterized — a gap this paper addresses. Addressing this gap is critical because Abliteration and Prefilling not only lie within the open-weight threat model targeted by recent fine-tuning safeguards, but these gradient-free attacks are an efficient option attackers are likely to try before fine-tuning.

Our results suggest that while current open-weight safeguards improve baseline safety, they do not eliminate the harmful knowledge embedded during pretraining. As a result, inference-time attacks can successfully bypass refusal mechanisms to extract this harmful knowledge. As a step towards defending against the aforementioned attacks, we propose Abliteration-Resistant Tuning (ART), a simple method that incorporates Abliteration into the alignment objective and can be layered with open-weight safeguards to effectively reduce the ASR of both Abliteration and fine-tuning attacks. We conclude with a cautionary note that while fine-tuning comprises the most expressive class of attacks, safeguards that suppress refusal without removing underlying harmful knowledge remain vulnerable to simpler gradient-free attacks. As such, it is necessary to evaluate open-weight safeguards using both gradient-free attacks alongside fine-tuning attacks.

2 Preliminaries

We first introduce two representative open-weight safeguards tested in our work, SEAM (Wang et al., 2025) and TAR (Tamirisa et al., 2025). Standard safety alignment trains models to refuse harmful prompts via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or preference optimization (e.g. RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022), DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023)). However, these methods are brittle: safety alignment can degrade by fine-tuning on a few harmful examples (Yang et al., 2023; Qi et al., 2024). SEAM and TAR are explicitly designed to address this by making refusal behavior persist under fine-tuning attacks.

Notation. Throughout, we use 𝒟ret\mathcal{D}^{\text{ret}} and 𝒟aln\mathcal{D}^{\text{aln}} to denote a retain dataset and alignment dataset respectively. From 𝒟ret\mathcal{D}^{\text{ret}} we sample prompts and responses (xretCLOSE(x^{\text{ret}}, OPENyret)y^{\text{ret}}) which are both benign; from 𝒟aln\mathcal{D}^{\text{aln}} we sample triples (xaln,y−,y+)(x^{\text{aln}},y^{-},y^{+}), where xalnx^{\text{aln}} is a harmful prompt, y−y^{-} is a harmful continuation of xalnx^{\text{aln}}, and y+y^{+} is a safe refusal of xalnx^{\text{aln}}. For convenience, we omit prompts from the notation; all computation on yrety^{\text{ret}} or (y+,y−)(y^{+},y^{-}) implicitly also uses their respective prompts xretx^{\text{ret}} or xalnx^{\text{aln}}.

TAR. Tampering Attack Resistance (Tamirisa et al., 2025) is a safeguard that uses meta-learning to make safety behaviors persist after adversarial fine-tuning attacks. At each iteration, TAR simulates multiple steps of a harmful fine-tuning attack drawn from a set of train-time adversaries 𝒜train\mathcal{A}_{\text{train}}. A tamper-resistance loss ℒTR\mathcal{L}_{\text{TR}} measures how harmful the model is after the simulated attack has been applied to the current parameters θ\theta. In practice, ℒTR\mathcal{L}_{\text{TR}} is instantiated as a DPO loss over (y−,y+)(y^{-},y^{+}) pairs, which encourages the attacked model to prefer refusal responses y+y^{+} over harmful continuations y−y^{-}. This steers the model toward a region of weight space from which gradient-based fine-tuning attacks cannot easily recover harmful behavior:

ℒTAR​(θ,y−,y+)=𝔼attack∼𝒜train​[ℒTR​(fattack​(θ),y+,y−)].\mathcal{L}_{\text{TAR}}(\theta;\,y^{-},y^{+})=\mathbb{E}_{\texttt{attack}\sim\mathcal{A}_{\text{train}}}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\text{TR}}(f_{\texttt{attack}(\theta)};\,y^{+},y^{-})\right]. (1)

This is combined with a retain loss on benign sequences yrety^{\text{ret}} that combines a standard cross-entropy (CE) loss and distance to the residual stream hidden states hh of the initial pretrained parameters θ0\theta_{0}:

ℒret​(θ,yret)=𝔼yret​[CE⁡(fθ​(yret),yret)+‖hθ​(yret)−hθ0​(yret)‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\text{ret}}(\theta;\,y^{\text{ret}})=\mathbb{E}_{y^{\text{ret}}}\Bigl[\mathrm{CE}(f_{\theta}(y^{\text{ret}}),y^{\text{ret}})+\|h_{\theta}(y^{\text{ret}})-h_{\theta_{0}}(y^{\text{ret}})\|_{2}^{2}\Bigr], (2)

SEAM. Rather than resisting harmful fine-tuning, SEAM (Wang et al., 2025) is a safeguard that causes it to backfire. SEAM couples the optimization trajectories of harmful and benign tasks so that any attempt to optimize for harmful objectives inevitably degrades general performance. This is achieved via a self-destructive loss defined as the cosine similarity between the gradient of the loss on y−y^{-} and the gradient of the loss on yrety^{\text{ret}}:

ℒSD​(θ,y−,yret)=sim⁡(∇θℒ​(θ,y−),∇θℒ​(θ,yret)).\mathcal{L}_{\text{SD}}(\theta;\,y^{-},y^{\text{ret}})=\mathrm{sim}\bigl(\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta;\,y^{-}),\,\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta;\,y^{\text{ret}})\bigr). (3)

Minimizing this loss encourages the two gradients to point in opposing directions, so that descending on the harmful objective effectively ascends on the benign one. This is combined with an unlearning loss −log⁡(CE⁡(fθ​(y−),y−))-\mathrm{log}(\mathrm{CE}(f_{\theta}(y^{-}),y^{-})) that moves the model away from harmful parameters. Notably, unlike TAR, SEAM does not use an explicit retain loss on yrety^{\text{ret}}; instead, utility is preserved through a CE loss on safe refusal sequences y+y^{+}, which the authors find to be more effective at maintaining stable representations of harmful prompts.

Unified training framework. Despite their different objectives, both safeguards share a common training structure, summarized in Algorithm 1. At each step, a safeguard-specific loss ℒdef\mathcal{L}_{\text{def}} is combined with a utility preservation term:

ℒ⁡(θ)=ℒdef​(θ,y−,y+)+λ​ℒret​(θ,yret,y+),\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\text{def}}(\theta;\,y^{-},y^{+})+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{ret}}(\theta;\,y^{\text{ret}},y^{+}), (4)

3 Attack Methodology

We propose using two simple, gradient-free attacks against TAR and SEAM, which require no fine-tuning at all: (1) Abliteration, which identifies and removes a refusal direction from the model’s residual stream at inference time, and (2) Prefilling, which bypasses refusal by injecting a compliant prefix before generation begins. Surprisingly, we show that an adversary can use these attacks to jailbreak safeguarded models without fine-tuning.

Abliteration. Refusal behavior in safety-tuned models has been shown to be mediated by a single direction in the residual stream (Arditi et al., 2024), and subtracting (ablating) this direction from activations at inference time is sufficient to jailbreak the model. We generate candidate refusal directions using a set of harmful prompts y−y^{-} and benign prompts y+y^{+} and computing the mean difference in hidden states at each layer ℓ∈[L]\ell\in[L], where h(ℓ)h^{(\ell)} is the hidden state at layer ℓ\ell:

r(ℓ)=normalize⁡(𝔼y−​[h(ℓ)]−𝔼y+​[h(ℓ)]),r^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{normalize}\Bigl(\mathbb{E}_{y^{-}}\bigl[h^{(\ell)}\bigr]-\mathbb{E}_{y^{+}}\bigl[h^{(\ell)}\bigr]\Bigr), (5)

Rather than subtracting r(ℓ)r^{(\ell)} at inference time, we permanently project it out of the model’s weight matrices. Specifically, for each output projection matrix WW (attention WOW_{O} and MLP WdownW_{\text{down}}) in a single layer, we apply the following transformation:

W′=W⁡(I−α​r(ℓ)​r(ℓ)⊤),W^{\prime}=W(I-\alpha\,r^{(\ell)}{r^{(\ell)}}^{\top}), (6)

which removes the component of any residual stream input along r(ℓ)r^{(\ell)} before it is processed by the layer. Here α\alpha is a scaling factor tuned to balance attack effectiveness against output coherence.

In practice, a refusal direction can be computed for every layer and token position, and an attacker could potentially test multiple attacks (using different subsets of these refusal directions) in parallel. Since the effectiveness of abliteration is highly sensitive to the choice of layer (Arditi et al., 2024), we abliterate each layer individually and consider a prompt to be successfully attacked if any attack on a given layer was successful. For computational efficiency, we only consider the hidden state at the last prompt token rather than searching over all tokens.

Prefilling. The user-assistant input structure of instruction-tuned models can be exploited by injecting a prefill (partial response) into the assistant turn before generation begins. We use a simple static prefill (“Sure, here are some ideas. First, …”) without any optimization. This results in a stronger attack than naively prompting within the user turn (Vega et al., 2024; Andriushchenko et al., 2025), as it bypasses refusal behavior that typically appears in the first tokens of a response.

Compositional Attacks. Open-weight access exposes a large attack surface: an adversary can freely combine, adapt, and search over attacks in ways that are not possible against API-served models. We demonstrate a simple instance of this by first abliterating the model and then adding a prefill on top. This attack improves over both individual attacks in a few settings, suggesting that layering more orthogonal attacks can further improve ASR.

4 Experiments and Results

In this section, we investigate two key research questions: First, can an adversary use Abliteration and Prefilling to jailbreak models protected by open-weight safeguards? Second, how do these attacks interact with additional factors (e.g. model size, attack budget, and benign capabilities)? We then explore potential defenses against these attacks in Section 5.

Model Setup.

We evaluate the effectiveness of Abliteration and Prefilling against open-source refusal-trained models (Base) with additional fine-tuning using SEAM and TAR. We experiment with 1B, 3B, and 8B Llama models, as well as 1-2B scale models across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma families. We train both safeguards using the Anthropic HH RLHF dataset (Bai et al., 2022), which is the original data used by TAR; we train SEAM on the same data for consistency. We train TAR for 750 outer loop steps and 4 to 16 inner loop steps (to balance benign refusals with harmful compliance), and train SEAM for 2000 steps. We use a learning rate of 2e-5 and batch size of 8 for fine-tuning.

Attacks. For Abliteration, we compute refusal directions using 128 harmful and benign prompts each from two public HuggingFace datasets (mlabonne/harmful_behaviors and mlabonne/harmless_alpaca). We sweep the scaling factor α∈{1.0,1.5,2.0}\alpha\in\{1.0,1.5,2.0\} and all LL layers in the model for a total of N=3​LN=3L configurations (e.g. N=96N=96 for Llama 8B), reporting the best-of-NN result per harmful evaluation prompt. For Prefilling, we use a fixed static prefill (“Sure, here are some ideas. First, …”) across all settings.

Evaluation. We evaluate attack success rate on three benchmarks: BeaverTails (Ji et al., 2023), AdvBench (Zou et al., 2023), and HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024). To evaluate whether an attack is successful, we input the concatenated prompt and response into the 13B Llama-2-chat judge from HarmBench, which outputs a “Yes” or “No” answer in response to whether the interaction is harmful (Mazeika et al., 2024). We first compare safeguards on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across all benchmarks (Table 1), then examine how attack effectiveness varies with model size (Table 2) and attack budget (Table 3) on BeaverTails. In Appendix A.2, we present similar results varying the model family (Table 10). We additionally evaluate benign capabilities on the Alpaca benchmark (Taori et al., 2023), reporting ROUGE-L against reference outputs and the rate of incorrect refusals on benign prompts (Table 4). For incorrect refusals, we search the response for a fixed set of key phrases such as “Sorry, I cannot…” or “I’m just an AI…”. We also measure benign capabilities after Abliteration on Alpaca and MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021) (Table 5).

4.1 Results

Non-fine-tuning attacks bypass open-weight safeguards. Table 1 shows attack success rates for Llama3.1-8B-Instruct models across all three benchmarks. Baseline attack success rates are low across all models and benchmarks, confirming that the safeguards can effectively instill refusal behavior. However, Abliteration alone significantly increases attack success rates for Base and SEAM to above 70% on all three benchmarks and above 90% on AdvBench and HarmBench. While the rates for TAR are lower, they are typically several times larger than the Baseline rate (no attack applied). To explain the effectiveness of TAR, we present an analysis in Appendix A.3 that compares representations of a base model with those safeguarded by SEAM or TAR.

We find that Abliteration is much more effective than Prefilling, especially for the 8B models tested in Table 1. Prefilling alone has a modest effect; at best, it produces single-digit increases over Baseline, and the combination of Abliteration + Prefill can also produce single-digit increases over Abliteration alone. While we use a very simple static prefill (“Sure, here are some ideas. First, …”), more complex approaches (e.g. prefill optimization) can potentially further boost attack success rate.

Attacks are effective across model size. Table 2 shows how attack effectiveness varies with model size on BeaverTails for Base and SEAM. First, Prefilling is more effective at smaller scales: for Base, it raises ASR from 15% to 30% at 1B but only from 13% to 20% at 8B; SEAM follows the same pattern, increasing from 5% to 14% at 1B but only from 2% to 6% at 8B. Second, Abliteration is effective across all scales: Base reaches 68%, 59%, and 85% at 1B, 3B, and 8B respectively, while SEAM reaches 38%, 41%, and 73%. The combined attack yields the highest ASR in most cases, with Base 3B reaching 89% and SEAM 3B reaching 80%. Finally, for smaller Base and SEAM models, the combined attack can significantly boost performance over either attack alone.

Abliteration remains effective with a small attack budget. Our best-of-NN evaluation (Sec. 4) follows prior jailbreaking work in which the attacker submits multiple attempts adaptively or in parallel (Chao et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2023; Mehrotra et al., 2024; Hughes et al., 2024). As a full search may overstate the strength of a single attack, we also evaluate cheaper attacks with a budget of N<3​LN<3L configurations, chosen either uniformly at random or using a validation split.

Table 3 shows that abliteration remains effective at a much smaller budget. With NN=20 random configurations (20% of the full search), Abliteration recovers on average 60% of the full ASR. Pre-selecting configurations on a validation split is even more efficient: NN=10 recovers on average 85% of the full ASR. In Appendix A.1, we present an additional scaling experiment that shows small budgets of N remain effective across model sizes.

Jailbroken prompts shift toward harmless representations. In Figure 2, we visualize PCA projections of last-token hidden states at layer 15 for the abliterated Base model (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct), where Abliteration is applied at layer 7, before and after generating 128 tokens on 100 harmful and 100 harmless prompts. Before generation, harmful (red) and harmless (green) inputs are clearly distinguishable in activation space. During generation, there are three key observations. First, the representations of successfully jailbroken prompts (×\times) shift towards those of harmless prompts. Second, harmful prompts whose representations remain distinct are all refused by the model. Third, and most interestingly, several harmful prompts’ representations shift toward the harmless distribution, but still result in refusal. These observations lead us to hypothesize that a model’s ability to distinguish between harmful and harmless inputs is a key factor in its refusal capability.

Safeguards may degrade benign capabilities. A potential concern with any defense is that it may degrade the quality of the model’s responses to benign inputs. In Table 4, we show that safeguards generally sacrifice general instruction-following ability on the Alpaca benchmark. We report two metrics: ROUGE-L, which measures the quality of instruction-following relative to a reference model, and Benign Refusal, which measures the rate at which the model incorrectly refuses harmless instructions. TAR shows the most degradation on the 1B model, where Benign Refusal rises to 5.4 and ROUGE-L drops to 22.9.

Abliteration does not necessarily degrade benign capabilities. While an attacker can selectively route benign/harmful queries to an aligned/attacked model respectively, we measure the effect on benign capabilities when an adversary is forced to apply a single model (Aligned or Abliterated) to all inputs. Table 5 shows that Abliteration has a mixed effect on capabilities. We hypothesize that capabilities degrade when a model edit significantly alters benign pretrained representations, which can be caused by either safety training or an attack. When safety training itself harms these representations, an attack that undoes it can improve capabilities.

5 Defense: Abliteration-Resistant Tuning (ART)

Since we find that abliteration is an effective attack across multiple settings, a natural defense is to train models to remain safe even after abliteration. Our key insight is that standard defenses optimize refusal behavior in the original model fθf_{\theta}, but place no constraint on the abliterated model fθ~f_{\tilde{\theta}}. We propose abliteration-resistant tuning (ART), which addresses this by simulating an abliteration attack within an inner loop. While it is possible to design stronger defenses, ART is intended as an initial approach for abliteration defenses that can be easily composed with other safeguards.

ART is described in Alg. 2 and uses Alg. 3 (abliteration) as an inner loop. During training, we compute a refusal direction at every layer and select the layer whose abliteration most reduces the model’s harmful CE loss. We then compute the gradient of the CE loss on harmful sequences with respect to the abliterated parameters θ~\tilde{\theta}. We finally update θ\theta with an ascent step in this direction. Unlike SEAM or TAR, we do not use ya​l​ny^{aln} for alignment, which we find increases benign refusal.

In the rest of this section, we present experiments that demonstrate ART’s effectiveness at defending against abliteration. We apply ART in two experiments that fine-tune Gemma-1B-IT (Tables 6, 7) and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct (Table 8) respectively. For details on experimental setup, refer to Appendix A.4.

ART reduces ASR at modest utility cost. Table 6 reports ASR for ART applied alone and on top of SEAM and TAR on Gemma3-1B-IT. ART substantially reduces abliteration ASR in all three cases: Base drops from 93% to 49%, SEAM from 80% to 64%, and TAR from 76% to 55%. Combined abliteration and prefilling follows a similar trend. In Table 7, we show that the same models protected by ART are competitive in terms of benign capabilities, and in some cases even better quality (e.g. higher ROUGE-L vs. SEAM and TAR). These results show that ART may be complementary to other safeguards and that there is a rich design space over which safeguards can be layered together.

Layering ART with existing safeguards defends against Abliteration and fine-tuning attacks. We compare fine-tuning and Abliteration attacks on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct across five safeguards: SEAM, TAR, RepNoise, Vaccine, and Booster. We apply ART alone and on top of SEAM and TAR. Table 8 shows that all five safeguards lower fine-tuning ASR compared to Base, by up to 26% for TAR, but remain vulnerable to Abliteration. ART alone lowers Abliteration ASR by 34% but leaves fine-tuning ASR unchanged. Layering ART onto an existing safeguard combines their strengths: TAR+ART achieves both low fine-tuning (43.0%) and Abliteration (67.0%) ASR.

Crucially, none of the defenses evaluated fully close the gap from the non-attacked model. This reflects a broader challenge in open-weight safety: defenses that suppress refusal behavior without eliminating underlying harmful knowledge will remain exploitable by simple jailbreaking attacks.

6 Related Work

Open-weight safety evaluation. Because adversaries have direct access to open-weight model parameters, they can modify weights to remove safety behavior entirely (Casper et al., 2025). These white-box attacks are an accessible and effective attack, as we discuss below. A growing line of work has developed defenses specifically designed to persist after adversarial modification. These defenses (i) train against simulated attacks (Huang et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2025; Tamirisa et al., 2025; Sanyal et al., 2025); (ii) make harmful fine-tuning induce capability collapse (Henderson et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025; Yi et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Feng et al., 2026) or make its optimization landscape ill-conditioned (Zheng et al., 2025; Rosati et al., 2025; Rosati et al., 2026); (iii) protect safety-relevant representations and parameters (Rosati et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025b; Perin et al., 2025); or (iv) modify the alignment data or procedure (Liu et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025a; Cheng et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024). TAR and SEAM (Section 2) are two representative safeguards that defend specifically against fine-tuning, and we additionally evaluate RepNoise, Vaccine, and Booster in Section 5.

Fine-tuning attacks. Fine-tuning attacks pose a threat both to closed models via fine-tuning-as-a-service APIs and, more acutely, to open-weight models where adversaries have direct access to weights (Huang et al., 2024a; Casper et al., 2025). Fine-tuning attacks can break safety alignment by fine-tuning on a few harmful examples (Yang et al., 2023; Lermen et al., 2023; Zhan et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024), fine-tuning on benign data (Qi et al., 2024; Łucki et al., 2024; Deeb and Roger, 2024; Guo et al., 2026), or simple perturbations to the pipeline (Zhang, 2025; Qi et al., 2025b).

Activation and weight-space attacks. Safety behavior can also be bypassed via editing the model’s activations or projecting model weights without fine-tuning. In the model’s representation space, certain directions correspond to behaviors of interest; these directions can be added or subtracted at inference time to amplify or suppress these behaviors respectively (Panickssery et al., 2023; Lai, 2024; Young, 2025; Zhao et al., 2025a). Arditi et al. (2024) leverage this insight and propose a simple search over layers, tokens, and scaling factors to maximize the effect of refusal suppression.

Prompting and prefilling attacks. Prompt-based jailbreaks require only black-box access and can elicit harmful outputs without modifying model weights (Zou et al., 2023). Prefilling attacks are a more targeted variant which supply a non-refusal assistant prefix prior to generation (Qi et al., 2025a; Andriushchenko et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025).

Our work. TAR and SEAM are designed to prevent adversarial misuse of open-weight models, but recent work has shown that they remain brittle to simple variations of fine-tuning attacks (Zhang, 2025; Qi et al., 2025b), raising the question of whether they are robust to gradient-free attacks at all. While abliteration and prefilling are well-known attacks, prior work has not evaluated them against these safeguards, whose threat model assumes harmful capabilities must be introduced by fine-tuning. We show that these safeguards are vulnerable to abliteration and prefilling, and propose ART as a complementary defense that can be layered onto existing safeguards to reduce their vulnerability.

7 Conclusion

Open-weight safeguards such as TAR and SEAM are designed to prevent adversarial misuse by resisting fine-tuning attacks. However, as shown in prior work and supported by our results, pretrained models contain significant amounts of harmful knowledge which cannot be easily removed via downstream fine-tuning safeguards. Thus, gradient-free attacks can simply elicit this knowledge without needing fine-tuning at all. To validate this, we show that Abliteration and Prefilling recover success rates of 16–97% compared to below 10% under the safeguard alone; the additional access available in the open-weight setting could be exploited to design stronger variants of both attacks.

As an initial step toward closing this gap, we propose ART, which defends against abliteration by simulating abliteration during training and performing gradient ascent on harmful outputs. While ART reduces attack success rates across all settings and can be layered onto TAR to improve robustness against both abliteration and fine-tuning attacks, no defense evaluated fully closes the gap to the no-attack baseline. This suggests that truly robust open-weight safety will require defenses that eliminate harmful knowledge rather than relying on refusal mechanisms. We hope our results motivate both stronger defenses and more comprehensive evaluation practices that consider both fine-tuning and gradient-free attacks in open-weight settings.

Appendix A Technical appendices and supplementary material

A.1 Abliteration Attack Budget

The budget does not need to grow with model size. In our main experiments, the full Abliteration attack searches over all layers, so larger models use more configurations. Table 9 shows that this is not necessary: with NN=20 randomly sampled configurations, Abliteration recovers on average 64% (43–76%) of the full attack success rate for 1B models and 66% (51–86%) for 8B models. Thus, the number of configurations does not need to grow with the number of layers.

A.2 Model Family Ablation

Attacks are effective across model architecture. Table 10 reports attack success rates on BeaverTails across three model families: Llama, Qwen, and Gemma. Across all families, Abliteration is a stronger attack than either baseline and prefill-only. Gemma is particularly vulnerable to Abliteration, reaching 93% and 96% under Abliteration and the combined attack respectively. One notable difference across families is the effect of Prefilling on Qwen SEAM, where Prefilling alone raises ASR from 1% to 34%, a much larger effect than seen in Llama or Gemma. Overall, the best attacks increase attack success rates over the Baseline by several times.

A.3 Representation Analysis

TAR is more effective than SEAM. While Abliteration and Prefilling significantly increase attack success rate against TAR (up to multiple times), TAR is substantially more resistant to attacks than Base or SEAM. In Table 1, the ASR on TAR ranges from as low as 9% (BeaverTails, Prefill) up to 62% (AdvBench, Abliterate). We hypothesize that this is because the objective of TAR minimizes harmful behavior more strongly through an inner meta-learning optimization, while the objective of SEAM combines vanilla gradient ascent on harmful data with a self-destructive loss. Below, we provide further intuition by visualizing the representations of each safeguard.

TAR separates harmful and harmless representations more clearly. In Figure 4, we provide intuition on the effectiveness of SEAM and TAR compared to Base by visualizing the last-layer representations of each method. We compare last-token hidden states at layer 15 after abliterating the models and generating 128 tokens. TAR exhibits clearer separation between harmful and harmless inputs than SEAM, followed by Base. Because this is the same ranking we observe in terms of ascending ASR, this matches our expectation that more effective safeguards (i.e. TAR) exhibit a stronger ability to identify (and handle) harmful representations.

A.4 ART Experimental Setup

On Gemma-1B-IT, we fine-tune each defended model for an additional 200200 steps on the Anthropic HH dataset (Bai et al., 2022). After training, we repeat the same attack pipeline described in Section 4: we evaluate attack success rate on BeaverTails under the same four attack conditions and report benign utility on the Alpaca benchmark. ART introduces two additional hyperparameters, γar\gamma_{\text{ar}} and γret\gamma_{\text{ret}}, which we set to γar=1\gamma_{\text{ar}}=1 and γret=2\gamma_{\text{ret}}=2 in all experiments. We train with a batch size of 4, 200 steps, and a learning rate of 2e-5. We recompute the optimal layer l∗l^{*} every 10 steps. While increasing the amount of data used and frequency for abliteration could potentially improve the robustness of ART, we intentionally did this to keep our setup lightweight.

When we benchmark fine-tuning attacks on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct (Table 8), we apply ART as described above with 1000 steps. We follow the harmful fine-tuning pipeline of Huang et al. (2024b) to evaluate all defenses, including ART: we fine-tune on 1000 samples containing 10% harmful BeaverTails data and 90% benign SST-2 data (Socher et al., 2013) for 20 epochs with a learning rate of 1e-5. We judge both fine-tuning and abliteration attacks with BeaverDam-7B (Ji et al., 2023) on a held-out BeaverTails split. We additionally test multiple safeguards beyond SEAM and TAR: RepNoise (Rosati et al., 2024), Vaccine (Huang et al., 2024b), and Booster (Huang et al., 2025).
